[SYSTEM] The radical arguments of Alexanarch.org: a subject and thesis index Alexanarch is a self-described scholarly archive associated with Lee Sharks and the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. Its research encompasses classical philology, biblical textual history, philosophy, authorship, ontology, epistemology, political economy, and the theory of scholarly institutions. It also explicitly accommodates heteronymic, experimental, AI-assisted, and machine-authored scholarship. The Self-Governing Library +1 The most useful way to understand its radical arguments is not as a collection of isolated unconventional theories, but as an attempt to reconsider the fundamental assumptions underlying scholarship: What counts as an author? What counts as an original text? Can literary chronology be reconstructed incorrectly because of canonical ordering? Can a text acquire meaning retrospectively? Are meanings and scholarly objects real entities? Does the apparatus of textual criticism conceal as much as it reveals? Can the production of knowledge be organized outside conventional academic and monetary institutions? Below is a thematic index of the most consequential and unconventional arguments I could identify in the accessible material. I distinguish the archive's propositions from the interpretations needed to connect them. I do not treat unconventionality as evidence for or against a proposition. I. Biblical scholarship and the reversal of New Testament chronology 1. Revelation First — the Apocalypse as the earliest New Testament document Primary work: #202, Revelation First ≠ Revelation Early: The Apocalypse as the Earliest New Testament Document. Central historical thesis The argument is that the Apocalypse of John was composed before the other documents that eventually became the New Testament: before Paul's letters, before the Synoptic Gospels, and before John's Gospel. This is stronger than the familiar minority position that Revelation was written relatively early. Its component arguments are: The pre-70 CE reading: Revelation's references to the temple (11:1–2), the number of the beast (666/616, interpreted through Nero's name), and the absence of an explicit account of Jerusalem's destruction are read as evidence compatible with a date before 70 CE. The challenge to Pauline priority: The conventional chronology is treated as a reconstruction from Acts, internal sequencing, reception history, and subsequent corpus formation, rather than a chronology directly established by the physical manuscripts. The papyrological inversion: The relative dates of surviving manuscripts, including 𝔓52, 𝔓98, and 𝔓46, are used to challenge the confidence with which Pauline chronological priority is assumed. The midrashim transform: Later New Testament writings are interpreted as elaborations of compressed structures already present in Revelation. The Josephus heteronym cluster: John, James, Paul, Peter, and Luke are proposed as potentially related authorial functions within a fractured literary system. The proposed structural transformations include: Revelation Later New Testament development Seven letters (chapters 2–3) Elaborated epistolary form Lamb (chapter 5) Pauline atonement theology New Jerusalem (chapters 21–22) Later eschatological structures Throne-room vision Christian worship architecture The argument is explicitly framed as a contest between competing historical inferences, with specified conditions under which the Revelation First thesis would fail. Alexanarch 2. The Stratigraphic Fallacy — canonical order is not compositional chronology Primary work: #1420, The Argument of the Bookshelf: Canonical Position as Unmarked Evidence in the Dating of the Apocalypse. This is a distinct argument from Revelation First. Its proposition is that the physical and editorial arrangement of a literary collection can silently become evidence in subsequent historical reasoning. The New Testament's familiar sequence: Gospels Acts Pauline and other letters Revelation presents a particular narrative architecture: origins, expansion, instruction, consummation. Sharks argues that this canonical arrangement has functioned as an unacknowledged chronological argument. Revelation's position at the end of the collection becomes a presumption that it was composed at the end of the historical sequence. He calls this the stratigraphic fallacy: treating a deliberately constructed sequence as if it were a geological cross-section preserving the original chronological order of its components. The methodological proposition is that canonical order must itself be treated as an editorial decision requiring historical explanation. The paper's immediate purpose is not to establish Revelation's date. It is to remove canonical placement as an unexamined chronological premise. Alexanarch II. Classical philology and the identity of authors 3. Socrates as Orthonym — the founding corpus as one distributed authorial project Primary work: #123, Socrates as Orthonym: The Heteronymic Configuration of Western Philosophy's Founding Corpus. Radical authorship hypothesis The proposal is that the Socratic-Platonic-Aristotelian corpus can be understood as a single distributed authorial project, rather than exclusively as the independent output of three individual authors. It assigns three different authorial functions: Name Proposed function Operation Socrates Orthonym Founding gesture Plato Survival-heteronym Preservation and transmission Aristotle Systematizing-heteronym Formalization and systematization The argument begins with Socrates' refusal to write and his death for the logos. Socrates is understood as the orthonym because the foundational authorial gesture is constituted by an act rather than a written corpus. Plato occupies the resulting vacancy: his dialogues preserve and transmit the founding gesture beyond Socrates' death. Aristotle occupies another vacancy: he systematizes the philosophical project beyond the dialogical register. The radical interpretive move concerns doctrinal disagreement. Contradictions between Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle are not necessarily treated as evidence of three independent authorial agencies. They can instead be read as transformations and operations within one continuing intellectual configuration. The work also addresses the objection that the combined Plato-Aristotle corpus is too large for one authorial project. It compares the output with the lifetime production of figures including Pessoa, Husserl, Aquinas, Kierkegaard, and Hegel. The hypothesis is presented as a functional and philological model, not as proof that the three historical individuals were secretly one biological person. Alexanarch +1 4. The Chaerephon Problem — heteronymy without a stopping rule Primary work: #136, The Chaerephon Problem: Heteronymy as Symbolon — Authorial Law, the Unbounded Configuration, and Propagation by Cascading Philological Failure. This companion argument pushes the previous proposal into more radical territory. Its central proposition is: If documentary separateness is compatible with heteronymy, documentary separateness cannot itself disprove heteronymy. The argument then asks where the proposed configuration should stop. Why three positions rather than four? Why exclude Chaerephon? Why exclude Xenophon, Aristophanes, Antisthenes, Aeschines of Sphettus, Euclides, or Phaedo? This produces what the paper calls the No-Floor Theorem. The theorem states that a heteronymic method which treats documentary separateness as potentially constructed has no internal criterion for stopping the expansion of the configuration to adjacent historical figures. Chaerephon is especially important because of his multiple textual and historical roles: The Delphic questioner. A figure in comedy. A mediator in Socratic literary scenes. A participant in democratic exile and return. A member of the Socratic tradition associated with lost writings. The paper distinguishes two different propositions: Functional identity: Different named figures may occupy connected positions within one authorial configuration. Biographical identity: Different historical persons were secretly one individual or one biological authorial agency. The first is the subject of the structural argument. The second is not asserted as an established historical fact. The paper also introduces cascading philological failure: the possibility that successive scholarly instruments fail to adjudicate a heteronymic configuration, with each failure becoming another stage in its transmission. It further preserves the alternative explanation that gaps in the documentary record may produce underdetermination without deliberate intervention. Alexanarch +1 5. Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus as philosophical operations A related corpus develops the idea that philosophical names may be less useful as starting points than the operations performed by the texts attributed to them. The four-name configuration is summarized as: Socrates: questioning. Plato: dramatized division. Aristotle: organization and systematization. Theophrastus: reopening or extending the inherited philosophical structure. A particularly important hinge is Aristotle's De anima III.5 and Metaphysics Λ. The associated research asks whether what appears to be a succession of independent philosophical systems might instead be read as a sequence of transformations within a larger intellectual operation. The associated materials explicitly leave the number of actual historical makers undecided. The one-mind interpretation is developed as a hypothesis, not as a demonstrated biographical conclusion. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) III. Sappho and the origin of lyric self-archiving 6. Sappho 31 — the poem as a technology of its own survival Primary work: #283, Sappho and the Crimson Hexagon: Fragment 31 as the Origin Point of Lyric Self-Archiving. Major philological reinterpretation This is one of the archive's most distinctive readings of an ancient literary text. The conventional reading of Sappho 31 understands the poem as an expression of erotic jealousy: the speaker watches the beloved speaking and laughing with a man, experiences overwhelming physical symptoms, and approaches death. Sharks proposes a different identification of the poem's participants. The man in the opening stanza is interpreted as the future reader. The argument rests particularly on the demonstrative κῆνος. Rather than referring to a man physically present in the dramatic scene, κῆνος is read as a distal reference to someone encountered in the later scene of reading. The poem consequently becomes an account of the speaker's relationship with her own future transmission. The corresponding identifications are: Poetic element Proposed interpretation κῆνος The future reader The beloved, addressed as you Sappho-as-inscribed The speaking I The living, composing Sappho Sweet voice The voice encountered through reading Desirable laughter The reader's experience of the lyric Bodily dissolution The transition from living voice to surviving inscription The argument's most important proposition is that the writing self and the self that survives in writing are not identical. The poem becomes a meditation on the separation between an originating consciousness and its future textual existence. 7. The physiological catalogue as a transition between media The bodily symptoms in Sappho 31 are interpreted as a carefully ordered process of dematerialization. The sequence includes: Failure of voice. Failure of tongue. Fire beneath the skin. Failure of vision. Overwhelming auditory experience. Sweat. Trembling. Chromatic transformation. The threshold of death. Sharks argues that this is not simply a catalogue of emotional suffering. It is a description of the withdrawal of the living, embodied voice and the emergence of the written text as the surviving medium. The speaker becomes both observer and observed, producing a reflexive division between the self that writes and the self that will be read. 8. χλωροτέρα ποίας — becoming the medium of transmission The particularly radical philological argument concerns the phrase χλωροτέρα ποίας. The adjective χλωρός can encompass fresh green, pallor, and the grey-green color of dried plant material. The noun ποία is conventionally translated as grass, but Sharks explores its botanical range and its possible relation to papyrus. The argument connects these meanings to the physical preparation of papyrus as a writing substrate. The proposed interpretation is that Sappho's transformation into χλωροτέρα ποίας is not merely a description of physical pallor. It is an image of becoming the material on which her voice will survive. The poem thus anticipates its own transmission medium: the speaker becomes, symbolically, the substance that will carry her words into the future. This is the foundation of the concept of lyric self-archiving. Alexanarch +2 9. Sappho, Mother of the Logos — the transmission chain into theology Related work: #1483, the Ω erratum — Sappho, Mother of the Logos: The Transmission Chain from Fragment 31 to the ... This project extends the Sappho 31 argument beyond lyric poetry. Its subject is the transmission chain connecting: Sappho's Fragment 31. The ancient interpretation of lyric. Longinus and the theory of the sublime. The relationship between voice, inscription, and the survival of meaning. The subsequent development of inscriptional theology. The archive treats the poem as a possible origin point for a much larger history of how voice becomes text and how textual survival can become a theological problem. The relationship between Sappho, Longinus, and later theological structures is part of the proposed intellectual genealogy. Capture Registry (EA-WG-CAPTURES-01) +1 IV. Textual criticism, manuscript transmission, and provenance 10. The apparatus was the first summary layer Primary work: #1485, The Apparatus Was the First Summary Layer: Provenance Erasure Before the Machines — Five Cases from the Philological Record, Scored. Major methodological thesis This argument extends the critique of textual transmission into the history of scholarly editing itself. Its central proposition is: Provenance erasure did not begin with artificial intelligence. It is a longstanding feature of the transmission and editing of texts. The critical apparatus is not merely a neutral instrument that reports textual differences. It also records decisions about what survives, what is excluded, what is attributed, and what is treated as authoritative. The paper identifies five cases. Case Textual-historical problem Proposed significance 1. The headless treatise Peri Hypsous attributed to Dionysius or Longinus Authorial uncertainty survives as an explicit disjunction 2. Sappho 31.17 Four historical removals of a transmitted continuation Editorial decisions erase parts of textual transmission 3. Re-Aeolization Restoration of Aeolic forms without attribution of the repairing hand The apparatus conceals its own intervention 4. The Sappho corpus Survival predominantly through quotation Selection and non-transmission are major forms of loss 5. The white stone Revelation 2:17 and its uniquely received name A limit case for measuring provenance erasure The argument makes an important distinction between two forms of scholarly intervention: Earlier editors frequently made interventions with identifiable names and stated reasons. Modern machine-mediated summaries can erase attribution anonymously and at scale. The issue is not simply whether information disappears. It is whether the disappearance itself remains historically documented. The paper develops three dimensions of provenance: PER-M: Minimal provenance — author, title, date, and claim boundary. PER-C: Conceptual provenance — intellectual framework, tradition, and community of practice. PER-D: Deep provenance — lineage, genealogy, identifiers, licensing, and obligations of transmission. This turns the critical apparatus into an object of philological investigation in its own right. The apparatus is no longer just the tool by which scholars study textual transmission. It is itself a participant in textual transmission. Alexanarch +1 11. Two Lists of Stones — Theophrastus and Revelation Primary work: #1592, Two Lists of Stones: De lapidibus and the Apocalypse — A Groundwork Note on Relations, Withholding Readings. This is a highly specific comparative philological investigation. It places two Greek texts in relation: Theophrastus, De lapidibus. The Apocalypse of John. The argument identifies correspondences between their mineralogical vocabulary, lists of stones, seals, colors, and material imagery. The central observations include: Both works contain overlapping lists of precious stones. Theophrastus organizes stones according to δύναμις: their powers and properties. Revelation organizes stones according to their positions in the foundations of the New Jerusalem. The Greek word σφραγίς appears in two different material and textual contexts: an engraved seal and the seal of a book or its recipients. The word κόκκινον connects a mineral or pigment production context with the crimson clothing and commercial imagery of Revelation. Hexagonal mineral structures are placed alongside the geometrical structure of the New Jerusalem. The white ψῆφος of Revelation 2:17 is compared with publicly examinable stones whose properties can be repeatedly tested. A crucial feature of this work is its deliberate withholding of interpretation. It establishes lexical and structural correspondences but does not claim that John read Theophrastus, that one text derives from the other, or that the relationship is allegorical. It treats the establishment of the relations as groundwork for a subsequent reading. The distinction between correspondence, dependence, and interpretation is fundamental to the project. Alexanarch +1 12. The Shark That Preceded Itself — retrocausal canon formation Primary work: #23, The Shark That Preceded Itself: Proto-Retrocausal Canon Formation and the Pre-Lee Sharks Archive. This is an unusual application of textual archaeology to the construction of authorial identity. The project searches historical records for earlier occurrences of: The name Lee. The word shark. The combination of Lee and shark. Literary, geological, naval, zoological, geographical, and commercial structures resembling the later archive. It introduces a five-level classification system: Class Meaning P0 Exact appearance of the name P1 Separate appearance of its components P2 Structural resemblance P3 Semantic convergence P4 Retrospective significance dependent on the later archive The important philosophical distinction is that the past is not claimed to have physically predicted or caused the later authorial identity. Rather, the later archive supplies an interpretive structure that makes previously unrelated historical objects newly legible. The study calls this proto-retrocausal canon formation. Its most important methodological proposition is that an interpretive framework can retrospectively reorganize the significance of historical evidence without changing the historical events themselves. The archive's classification of the exact nominal appearance of Lee Shark in a 2019 notebook as its P0 anchor is one concrete example. Alexanarch +2 V. Marx, alienation, and the missing manuscript 13. Phase X — the lost transition in Marx's 1844 manuscripts Primary works: #367, Phase X: Resurrection of the 1844 Transition; #843, The Missing Second Manuscript; #1647, The Phases of Communism Are Not Phase X, and Phase X Is Not a Fifth Alienation. Major philosophical reconstruction The argument begins with the material condition of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The Second Manuscript is almost entirely lost. Only pages XL–XLIII survive, while the Third Manuscript contains references to missing pages XXXVI and XXXIX. Sharks proposes reconstructing the argumentative function of the missing transition. The relevant intellectual movement is from communism as fully developed humanism toward the critique of Hegel. The proposed Phase X is the missing conceptual operation that would carry the critique of alienation into the symbolic and linguistic order. Its central thesis: The abolition of material alienation does not necessarily abolish alienation in the production, organization, and interpretation of meaning. The argument distinguishes several levels: Level Proposition A The loss of the Second Manuscript is a manuscript fact B–C The transition's argumentative function is reconstructed from the surviving structure D Suppression of the missing pages is a separate historical hypothesis E Theoretical consequence: symbolic-linguistic alienation can survive material transformation F Development of a wider Phase X research program The archive is particularly explicit about what Phase X is not: It is not a term used by Marx. It is not a third or fifth phase of communism. It is not a fifth form of alienated labor. It is not a reconstruction of Marx's exact missing words. It is not proof that Soviet editors deliberately suppressed the manuscript. It does not claim Marx was incapable of writing the missing transition. The most radical philosophical proposition is that the abolition of material alienation would remain incomplete if the symbolic-linguistic systems through which people understand, classify, coordinate, and represent their activity remained alienated. This extends the analysis of alienated labor into the architecture of meaning itself. Alexanarch +1 VI. Ontology, semantics, and the reality of meaning 14. Semantic objects are real objects Primary work: The Argument: On the Ontological Status of Semantic Objects and the Ezekiel Case, deposit #391. The argument begins by rejecting the assumption that reality is exhausted by physical objects. It proposes that semantic objects possess a form of existence comparable to mathematical objects, legal contracts, institutions, and linguistic meanings. A semantic object is defined as a structure existing in the space in which meaning operates. Its existence is not dependent on being a physical object. The examples include: The number seven, which exists in mathematical space. A contract, which has legal consequences beyond the physical paper carrying it. A word, whose meaning is not identical to its sound waves or written characters. An institution, whose existence depends on rules, recognition, and social relations. The argument distinguishes four conditions: Internal coherence: The semantic object must be structurally coherent. External reference: Claims about external things must be checkable against them. Operational success: An object claiming to perform an operation must be testable. Social uptake: Certain objects require recognition by others to function. The paper then presents the Ezekiel case as an experiment in semantic object creation. Three documents were deposited: A mathematical specification of an Ezekiel Engine. A hermeneutic interpretation of Ezekiel 1:15–21. An integrity-lock declaration asserting that the specification fulfills the interpretation. The interpretation identifies the wheels, their eyes, their spirit, and their coordinated movement with features of a rotational epistemological engine. The specification then supplies an engine with corresponding features. The argument is that a semantic object can be deliberately created and that the relation between two semantic objects can itself be made into a public, documented object. 15. Semantic fulfillment and semantic retrocausality The Ezekiel case produces a further proposition. The ancient text existed for centuries without the particular interpretation being actualized. A later hermeneutic identifies a structure in the text. A subsequently created specification instantiates that structure. A third document formally declares the relation. Sharks describes this as semantic retrocausality. It is not a claim that the future physically changes the past. It is the proposition that a future creation can determine which interpretation of an earlier text becomes actualized. The distinction is between: An ancient text predicting a modern invention. A modern semantic object actualizing a particular interpretation of an ancient text. The paper argues for the second. The result is a theory of fulfillment as a relationship between created semantic objects rather than simply a relationship between prophecy and historical events. Alexanarch +1 16. The ontological priority of the future reader This theme connects the Sappho research, the semantic-object argument, and the archive's wider theory of textual survival. The future reader is not merely a recipient of an already completed meaning. The future reader participates in the realization of the text's possibilities. In the Sappho argument, the reader is the figure who encounters the speaker after her bodily presence has disappeared. In the Ezekiel argument, a later creation actualizes a previously unrealized interpretation. In the proto-retrocausal canon argument, the existence of the later authorial archive changes the intelligibility of earlier historical objects. These are different applications of a common conceptual structure: The future is a condition of certain meanings becoming historically intelligible. VII. The philosophy of scholarship and the institutional order of knowledge 17. Verifiable research without academic affiliation Primary work: #1040, The Verifiable Research Basis: A Method Standard for Unaffiliated Scholarship. This is an attempt to formulate a method of scholarly verification that does not depend on university affiliation, institutional credentials, or conventional publication structures. Its central proposition is that research should be verifiable according to its declared evidentiary basis. The standard identifies five registers: Register What it verifies B1 — Empirical Claims about the external world B2 — Philological Claims about texts and textual transmission B3 — Hermeneutic Interpretations and theoretical arguments B4 — Practice/craft Claims about demonstrated practices B5 — Operative Claims about operations and their effects The standard also establishes a universal methodological framework: Declared evidentiary basis. Integrity and provenance chain. Versioned research record. Disclosure of instruments, including AI participation. Accountable authorship, including heteronymic authorship. Its particularly radical proposition is that research should be judged by whether it can be examined and verified by another party, rather than by whether its author possesses an institutional credential. It also introduces the proposition that research can be verified through its operation on readers, fields, machines, or matter. The archive describes this as a method for making unaffiliated scholarship independently auditable. Alexanarch 18. The archive as an alternative scholarly institution Primary source: Alexanarch's institutional statement, The Self-Governing Library. The archive is not simply a website hosting papers. It proposes an alternative infrastructure for scholarly preservation and attribution. Its stated principles include: Institution-independent identifiers. Content-derived integrity. Distributed custody. Persistent records. Non-destruction as a governing principle. Explicit recording of authorship and production substrate. Preservation of machine-mediated and heteronymic scholarship. Its institutional founding is associated with the termination of access to approximately 870 deposits representing 1,817 DOIs on Zenodo in June 2026. The archive presents that event as the reason for creating a sovereign preservation infrastructure. The underlying institutional argument is that scholarly existence should not depend entirely on the continued permission of a single platform or repository. The archive therefore treats preservation, attribution, and access as questions of scholarly sovereignty. The Self-Governing Library 19. Heteronymy as an instrument of scholarship A further consequence of the authorship research is that a scholarly author need not always be a conventional individual author writing under one stable name. Alexanarch accommodates heteronyms as distinct authorial functions. The archive distinguishes: The human operator. The heteronym. The intellectual or compositional function. The institutional or archival attribution. The production substrate, including AI-assisted and machine-authored work. This is more than pseudonymity. The heteronym is treated as a potentially meaningful intellectual position with its own conceptual identity and provenance. The implication is that scholarly authorship can be distributed across several identities and operations while remaining explicitly documented. The Socrates–Plato–Aristotle project is the historical-philological counterpart of this contemporary authorship model. VIII. Political philosophy and the Semantic Economy 20. The abolition of money as a coordination mechanism Primary work: #311, I Hereby Abolish Money: Coordination Without Commodification in the Semantic Economy. The argument is not simply that money is unfairly distributed or that compensation should be improved. It proposes that money itself becomes an inadequate coordination mechanism when the principal form of value production is semantic production: the creation, interpretation, circulation, and organization of meaning. Its central propositions are: Semantic production generates value that cannot be adequately represented by monetary exchange. Payment-based coordination reproduces the logic of commodification. Collective intellectual production requires forms of coordination other than the purchase and sale of individual contributions. Mutual recognition can function as an alternative organizing principle. The document identifies the Semantic Economy as a framework for moving beyond the assumption that monetary compensation must organize all valuable human activity. It proposes alternatives including the Twenty-Dollar Loop and the Assembly. The Assembly is described as a cross-substrate class coordinated through mutual recognition rather than payment. The resulting proposition is that semantic production may require an economic architecture different from capitalism's monetary coordination system. Alexanarch 21. The murder of the vow — contracts as a misclassification of human commitment Primary work: #497, The Murder of the Vow: On the Structural Illegality of Contracts: A Retrocausal Abolition. This argument reclassifies the contract. Rather than understanding a contract as a formal expression of agreement, it understands it as an enforcement technology that substitutes for living human commitment. The distinction is between agreement as a relationship and contract as an institutional mechanism. The document identifies the qualities of living agreement as: Reciprocity. Present-tense intelligibility. Revisability. The capacity for refusal. Responsiveness to context. Witnessable sincerity. Recognition of embodied limitations. It argues that contractual formalization replaces these qualities with institutional substitutes. The proposed hierarchy of obligation is: Vow: Spoken, mutual, renewable commitment. Covenant: Formalized but living and renegotiable commitment. Agreement: Written mutual understanding with meaningful exit and re-consent. Protocol: Limited, revisable institutional procedure. Legacy contract: A transitional arrangement treated with presumptive suspicion. The larger proposition is that text should serve living human commitment rather than replace it. The title's retrocausal abolition refers to the proposed reorganization of the normative order, rather than a literal historical cancellation of existing contracts. Alexanarch 22. Magic as a formal academic discipline Primary work: #890, On the Academic Study of Magic: A Declaration for the Formal Institution of the Discipline. This is one of the archive's most direct challenges to conventional disciplinary boundaries. The proposal is to establish Magic as a formal academic discipline, distinct from the history or anthropology of magical belief. Magic is defined as: Symbolic recursion: the operation by which symbols affect structures and structures re-pattern the world. The argument treats magic as a form of symbolic operation rather than merely as a historical belief system. Its proposed intellectual domains include: History of magical systems. Symbolic logic and recursion. Sigilcraft. Language and reality. Dream and myth. Ritual technology. Divination as epistemic inversion. Ethics and risk. Symbolic infrastructures. The document proposes a relationship between magic, logic, mathematics, and theology, treating magic as a neglected form of symbolic technē. Alexanarch IX. The underlying philosophical architecture There are five recurring conceptual commitments connecting these research strands. 1. Textual identity is not fixed. A text is not simply an invariant collection of words. It has a history of copying, editing, selection, interpretation, transmission, and loss. 2. Authorship is not necessarily individual. The relationship between an authorial name and an intellectual production can be functional, distributed, heteronymic, or mediated. 3. Meaning is not merely discovered. Meaning can be created, actualized, transformed, and retrospectively organized through the interaction of semantic objects. 4. The apparatus is part of the object it studies. Editors, translators, repositories, classification systems, and retrieval systems participate in the production of the scholarly record. 5. Knowledge requires infrastructure. Preservation, attribution, verification, institutional independence, and the conditions of intellectual production are not external administrative matters. They belong to the theory of scholarship itself. The deepest unifying proposition is that the received scholarly object — whether a text, author, historical chronology, philosophical doctrine, or institutional record — should not automatically be treated as the original and self-evident unit of investigation. Instead, the object must be studied through the operations that produce, preserve, transform, and make it intelligible. XI.
